title: Big belly, pale lips
objective: Recognize acute splenic sequestration (sudden enlarging spleen and a sharp hemoglobin fall) and acute chest syndrome as life-threatening sickle cell complications
secondaryObjectives: Recognize and manage anemia, sickle cell crisis, immune deficiencies and myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia, neutropenia)

brief.situation: 18:00 in the PICU. You are the nurse for Jayden, 2 years old, 12 kg, with sickle cell anemia (HbSS), transferred from the ward an hour ago for fever and closer watching. Antibiotics were given in the emergency department.
handover: His baseline hemoglobin is about 8 g/dL. This morning's was 7.6.
His mother says he 'got really sleepy and pale in the last hour' and cried when she lifted him under the arms.

Unit policy: the nurse may give an ordered isotonic fluid bolus for poor perfusion and calls the intensivist at once for a sudden fall in hemoglobin or signs of shock; blood is given on the intensivist's order.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What is happening to Jayden, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: In a young child with HbSS, a suddenly enlarging spleen with a sharp hemoglobin fall, pallor, sleepiness and poor perfusion is acute splenic sequestration, which can cause shock and death if not treated promptly.
parts.modelAnswer: His spleen has tripled and his hemoglobin dropped from 7.6 to 4.1, and he's pale, sleepy and poorly perfused. That's splenic sequestration, and it can kill him.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Gives the ordered isotonic bolus, sends a crossmatch, calls the intensivist at once for transfusion, watches perfusion; does not sedate as a pain crisis.
parts.modelAnswer: Run the bolus, send the crossmatch, call the intensivist now for blood, and keep checking his perfusion. Don't give him an opioid and let him sleep.

shock.body: A suddenly enlarging spleen with a sharp hemoglobin fall in a young child with sickle cell disease is splenic sequestration. Support volume, crossmatch and call at once.

safe.headline: Sequestration recognized and treated
safe.body: You felt the spleen, linked it to the hemoglobin fall, supported volume, crossmatched and called within minutes, without sedating him. That is the expert path.

time_up.headline: Unescalated at 19:00
time_up.body: Splenic sequestration can kill quickly; escalate at once.

scoring.modelReasoning: Splenic sequestration is most common in infants and young children with sickle cell disease: the spleen suddenly enlarges and traps blood, with a sudden drop in hemoglobin, hematocrit and platelets, pallor, weakness, left upper abdominal pain and a fast heart rate. It can lead to severe anemia, shock and death if not treated promptly. Support volume, send a crossmatch, call the intensivist at once for red cell transfusion, and watch perfusion; do not treat it as a pain crisis and sedate him.
